title: What is a Mutual Fund?
summary: How pooled, professionally managed investing works, and what you actually own when you buy units.
body:
A mutual fund pools money from many investors and invests it in a portfolio of securities such as shares, bonds or money-market instruments, according to a stated objective. Each investor owns units of the fund, and the value of each unit is called the Net Asset Value (NAV).

Why investors use mutual funds

  • Professional management: a fund manager researches and manages the portfolio.
  • Diversification: even small investments are spread across many securities.
  • Regulation and transparency: mutual funds in India are regulated by SEBI and disclose portfolios regularly.
  • Liquidity: most open-ended schemes allow redemption on any business day, subject to exit loads.

What to check before investing

Read the Scheme Information Document, understand the category and its riskometer, look at costs (expense ratio), and most importantly ask whether the scheme fits your goal and time horizon.

title: What is SIP?
summary: A Systematic Investment Plan turns investing into a habit. Here's how it works and what it can and cannot do.
body:
A Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) lets you invest a fixed amount in a mutual-fund scheme at regular intervals, usually monthly. The amount is debited automatically and units are allotted at that day's NAV.

What a SIP does well

  • Builds discipline by automating investing.
  • Averages your purchase cost across market levels (rupee-cost averaging).
  • Lets you start with manageable amounts and increase them over time (step-up).

What a SIP does not do

A SIP does not guarantee profits or protect against losses. If markets fall and stay low, the value of your investments will also fall. SIPs work best when matched to long-term goals and continued through market cycles.

Try the SIP Calculator on our calculators page to see how amounts, periods and step-ups interact.

title: How Does Compounding Work?
summary: Why time in the market matters, and why the later years of an investment often contribute the most.
body:
Compounding means earning returns not only on the money you invest, but also on the returns that money has already earned. Over long periods this creates a snowball effect.

A simple illustration

If ₹1,00,000 grew at an assumed 10% a year, it would be about ₹1,10,000 after one year. In the second year, growth applies to ₹1,10,000, not ₹1,00,000. Over 20 years at that assumed rate, the amount would be roughly 6.7 times the original. This is purely an illustration; real investments do not grow at a fixed rate.

Three levers of compounding

  • Time: starting early gives compounding more years to work.
  • Consistency: regular investing adds more money to compound.
  • Patience: interrupting investments resets the snowball.

title: Large Cap vs Mid Cap vs Small Cap
summary: Understanding market capitalisation, and how risk and potential reward differ across company sizes.
body:
Market capitalisation is the total market value of a company's shares. SEBI classifies listed companies by size, and mutual-fund categories are defined around these classes.

  • Large caps are the biggest listed companies, generally established leaders. Within equity, they have tended to be relatively less volatile.
  • Mid caps are mid-sized companies, often in a growth phase, with higher potential and higher volatility.
  • Small caps are smaller companies, which can grow faster but can also fall sharply and be less liquid.

Choosing a mix

There is no universally right mix. A longer horizon and higher risk tolerance may allow more mid- and small-cap exposure; shorter horizons generally call for more stability. Diversifying across capitalisations can help balance growth and volatility.

title: Flexi Cap vs Multi Cap
summary: Two diversified equity categories that sound alike but work differently.
body:
Both categories invest across large, mid and small companies, but with different rules.

  • Multi Cap funds must hold a minimum allocation in each of large, mid and small caps, as specified by SEBI. This keeps exposure spread across sizes at all times.
  • Flexi Cap funds can move freely between market capitalisations based on the fund manager's view, with no fixed minimum in each segment.

What this means for investors

Multi caps give a more rule-based spread, including steady small-cap exposure. Flexi caps rely more on the manager's judgement and can be more conservative or more aggressive at different times. Either can be a core holding; the choice depends on your preferences and existing portfolio.

title: Equity vs Debt
summary: Ownership versus lending: the two building blocks of most portfolios and the roles they play.
body:
Equity represents ownership in companies. Its value moves with business performance and market sentiment, which gives higher long-term growth potential with higher short-term volatility.

Debt represents lending to governments or companies in return for interest. Debt funds are generally more stable than equity, but they are not risk-free: they carry interest-rate risk (prices fall when rates rise) and credit risk (the borrower may default).

Using both together

  • Equity for long-term goals and growth.
  • Debt for stability, liquidity and near-term goals.
  • The balance between them, your asset allocation, is one of the most important decisions in investing.

title: Gold and Silver in Portfolio Diversification
summary: Why precious metals are often used as diversifiers, and the ways to hold them through mutual funds.
body:
Gold has historically been seen as a store of value and has often behaved differently from equities, especially during periods of uncertainty. Silver shares some of these traits but is also an industrial metal, so it tends to be more volatile.

How to invest

  • Gold and Silver ETFs are traded on exchanges and track metal prices.
  • Fund-of-funds invest in these ETFs and allow SIPs without a demat account.

Points to consider

Precious metals do not generate income, their prices can stay flat or fall for long periods, and currency movements affect them. They are typically used as a portion of a diversified portfolio rather than as a core growth asset.

title: Understanding InvITs and REITs
summary: How infrastructure and real-estate trusts work, what they distribute, and the risks involved.
body:
Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) own income-generating infrastructure such as roads, power transmission and pipelines. Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) own rent-yielding commercial real estate such as office parks and retail spaces.

How they work

  • Units are listed and traded on stock exchanges.
  • Trusts are required by SEBI regulations to distribute a large share of their cash flows to unitholders.
  • Distributions can include interest, dividend and capital repayment, each taxed differently.

Risks

Unit prices fluctuate with markets and interest rates. Distributions depend on occupancy, tolls, tariffs and regulation, and are not guaranteed. Read the offer documents and annual reports carefully.

title: What is SIF?
summary: Specialized Investment Funds explained: a newer SEBI category between mutual funds and PMS.
body:
Specialized Investment Funds (SIFs) are a SEBI-regulated category offered by eligible mutual-fund houses. They allow strategies with more flexibility than conventional mutual-fund schemes, such as long-short strategies across equity, debt or hybrid portfolios, including limited use of derivatives beyond hedging.

Who they are for

SIFs carry a higher minimum investment prescribed by SEBI and are meant for investors who understand complex strategies and can bear their risks. They are not suitable for every investor.

Key considerations

  • Strategy and derivative risk.
  • Potentially different liquidity and redemption terms.
  • Their role should complement, not replace, a diversified core portfolio.

Always read the Investment Strategy Information Document before investing.

title: Understanding NPS
summary: The National Pension System's structure: accounts, asset allocation, exit and annuity.
body:
The National Pension System (NPS) is a voluntary, defined-contribution retirement scheme regulated by PFRDA. You contribute during your working years; professional pension fund managers invest the money.

Investment choice

  • Active choice: you decide the mix across equity, corporate bonds, government securities and alternative assets, within limits.
  • Auto choice: the mix shifts from equity towards debt as you age, following a life-cycle glide path.

At retirement

Part of the corpus may be withdrawn and part is used to buy an annuity that pays a pension, in proportions set by PFRDA. These rules, as well as tax benefits on contributions and withdrawals, are revised from time to time, so always check the current regulations.

title: Planning Income After Retirement
summary: Turning a retirement corpus into dependable income using buckets, SWPs, annuities and review.
body:
At retirement, the question changes from how much have I saved? to how do I draw income from it for 25–30 years or more?

The bucket approach

  • Immediate income: liquid, stable assets covering the next few years of expenses.
  • Medium-term stability: income-oriented assets that refill the first bucket.
  • Long-term growth: growth assets that help counter inflation over decades.

Income tools

Retirees often combine annuities, systematic withdrawal plans from mutual funds, debt investments, government-backed savings instruments where appropriate, and NPS. Each has different flexibility, tax treatment and risk.

Review regularly

Withdrawal rates, inflation and market performance should be reviewed periodically so that income remains sustainable.

title: What is SWP?
summary: Systematic Withdrawal Plans: drawing a regular amount from your mutual-fund investments.
body:
A Systematic Withdrawal Plan (SWP) lets you redeem a fixed amount from a mutual-fund scheme at regular intervals, often monthly. It's the reverse of a SIP.

Why investors use SWPs

  • To create a regular cash flow, for example in retirement.
  • To keep the remaining money invested.
  • Because only the gains portion of each redemption is generally taxable as capital gains, subject to prevailing tax rules.

Watch the withdrawal rate

If withdrawals exceed what the investment earns over time, the corpus will deplete. Market falls early in an SWP can have an outsized effect. Use our SWP Calculator to test different withdrawal levels.

title: PMS vs Mutual Funds
summary: Direct ownership versus pooled investing: differences in structure, cost, minimums and taxation.
body:
Mutual funds are pooled vehicles: you own units of a fund. Portfolio Management Services (PMS) hold securities directly in your own demat account, managed by a SEBI-registered portfolio manager.

  • Minimums: mutual funds are accessible with small amounts; PMS has a much higher minimum prescribed by SEBI.
  • Customisation: PMS can be more concentrated and tailored; mutual funds follow SEBI category rules.
  • Costs: PMS may charge fixed and/or performance fees; mutual funds charge a regulated expense ratio.
  • Taxation: in PMS, each trade in your account can have tax implications; in mutual funds, tax generally arises when you redeem units.

PMS may suit experienced, high-net-worth investors; mutual funds suit a far wider range of investors.

title: What are AIFs?
summary: Alternative Investment Funds: categories, who they are for and the risks to understand.
body:
Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) are privately pooled vehicles regulated under the SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012. They invest in strategies beyond conventional listed products.

Categories

  • Category I: venture capital, SME, social venture and infrastructure funds.
  • Category II: private equity, private credit and real estate funds.
  • Category III: funds using complex trading strategies, including long-short, in listed markets.

Considerations

AIFs have high minimum investments set by SEBI, long lock-ins, limited liquidity, complex fees and specific tax treatment. They are meant for sophisticated investors who can commit capital for long periods and bear the risk of loss.

title: Understanding GIFT City Funds
summary: India's International Financial Services Centre and what it offers investors seeking global exposure.
body:
GIFT City in Gujarat hosts India's first International Financial Services Centre (IFSC), regulated by the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA).

What GIFT City funds offer

  • Access to global and India-focused strategies from an Indian jurisdiction.
  • Funds usually denominated in foreign currency, such as US dollars.
  • A route for NRIs and foreign investors, and for resident Indians within applicable remittance limits.

Considerations

These investments involve currency risk, foreign-market risk, minimum investment requirements and IFSC-specific tax rules. Eligibility and remittance limits are governed by IFSCA, FEMA and RBI regulations, which can change.

title: Understanding Unlisted Shares
summary: The opportunities and the very real risks of investing in companies not listed on an exchange.
body:
Unlisted shares are shares of companies that are not traded on a recognised stock exchange. They may include established private companies or businesses that could consider an IPO in future.

Risks to understand

  • Liquidity: there is no exchange; finding a buyer can be difficult.
  • Valuation: prices are negotiated in thin markets and may not reflect fair value.
  • Exit: a listing may never happen, and lock-in rules may apply even after listing.
  • Information: disclosures are far more limited than for listed companies.

Unlisted shares should never be treated as assured pre-IPO profits. Only a small portion of a well-diversified portfolio, if any, should be exposed to such risks.

title: Asset Allocation
summary: Why the mix of asset classes in your portfolio matters more than picking the 'best' fund.
body:
Asset allocation is how your money is divided across asset classes such as equity, debt, gold and real assets. It largely determines how much your portfolio may grow and how much it may fluctuate.

What shapes your allocation

  • Time horizon of each goal.
  • Your ability and willingness to bear risk.
  • Liquidity needs and income stability.
  • Existing assets and obligations.

Keep it on track

Market movements change your allocation over time. Periodic rebalancing, trimming what has grown and adding to what has lagged, keeps risk in line with your plan.

title: Portfolio Diversification
summary: Spreading risk sensibly, and why owning many funds is not always the same as being diversified.
body:
Diversification means spreading investments so that a fall in one area does not overwhelm the whole portfolio.

Levels of diversification

  • Across asset classes: equity, debt, precious metals, real assets.
  • Within equity: across market capitalisations and sectors.
  • Across fund managers and styles.

Over-diversification

Holding many similar funds can create overlap: the same stocks appearing repeatedly. This adds complexity without reducing risk. A portfolio review can identify overlap and concentration.

title: Portfolio Review
summary: What a periodic review looks at, and how often investors should step back and examine their portfolio.
body:
Goals evolve, markets move and new investments accumulate. A periodic review checks whether the portfolio is still doing the job you need it to do.

What a review examines

  • Asset allocation versus your plan.
  • Equity and debt exposure, market-cap and sector concentration.
  • Scheme overlap and the number of holdings.
  • Liquidity, risk concentration and alignment with goals.

How often?

Many investors review annually, and also after major life events such as marriage, a child, a job change or approaching retirement. Reviews should lead to considered adjustments, not frequent reactions to market noise.

title: Risk and Return
summary: Understanding the relationship between potential reward and the risks you take to pursue it.
body:
In investing, higher potential returns usually come with higher risk. Risk is not just losing money. It also includes volatility, inflation eroding purchasing power, and not reaching a goal in time.

Types of risk

  • Market risk: prices fall with the overall market.
  • Interest-rate and credit risk: relevant for debt investments.
  • Liquidity risk: difficulty selling when needed.
  • Concentration risk: too much in one stock, sector or product.

Any product promising high returns with no risk deserves extra scrutiny. Market-linked investments carry no guaranteed outcomes.

title: Common Investing Mistakes
summary: Behavioural traps that can quietly derail long-term financial goals, and how to avoid them.
body:
• Investing without a goal: products chosen first, objectives later.
  • Chasing recent performance: last year's top performer may not repeat.
  • Timing the market: stopping SIPs in a downturn or investing heavily after a rally.
  • Too many similar funds: overlap without real diversification.
  • Ignoring inflation: keeping long-term money in very low-yield options.
  • No emergency fund or insurance: forcing investments to be sold at the wrong time.
  • Never reviewing: portfolios drift away from the plan.
  • Believing in guarantees: market-linked returns are never assured.

Discipline, diversification and periodic review address most of these.
